title: Energy Drinks and Alcohol: Why the Mix Is Riskier Than You Think
excerpt: Mixing energy drinks with alcohol makes you feel less drunk, not less impaired. What 'wide-awake drunk' means, caffeine by brand, heart and sleep risks, and whether Red Bull has alcohol.
metaDescription: Energy drinks with alcohol make you feel less drunk, not less impaired. Wide-awake drunk explained, caffeine by brand, heart risks, and Red Bull FAQs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** mixing energy drinks with alcohol doesn't make you less drunk. It makes you *feel* less drunk. The caffeine covers up the drowsiness that normally tells you to slow down, while your blood alcohol, reaction time, and judgment are just as impaired as they would be without it. Researchers call this being "wide-awake drunk," and it's the main reason vodka Red Bulls, Jägerbombs, and similar drinks have a worse safety record than the alcohol alone would suggest. Add the extra strain on your heart and your sleep, and the combination is one of the riskier ways to drink. (For coffee, tea, and caffeine in general, see our [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) guide.)

**The quick rules:** If you're going to drink, the safest choice is to skip the energy drink as a mixer. If you do have one, count it as a full serving of caffeine, keep it to one, and don't use it to "stay out longer." Pace your drinks by the clock and by count, not by how alert you feel, because that feeling is exactly what the caffeine distorts. Never drive after mixing them, even if you feel sharp. And if your heart starts racing or pounding irregularly, stop drinking and caffeine for the night.

> **When to get help.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you or a friend has chest pain or pressure, a very fast or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, fainting, trouble breathing, a seizure, confusion, repeated vomiting, or can't be woken up. Those can be signs of a heart rhythm problem or alcohol poisoning, and they need care right away. If you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, anxiety disorder, or take prescription medicine (especially stimulants for ADHD or antidepressants), talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining caffeine and alcohol.

## Why Energy Drinks and Alcohol Are a Risky Mix

Alcohol and caffeine push your body in opposite directions, but not evenly. Alcohol is a depressant. It slows reaction time, loosens judgment, and, as the night goes on, makes you sleepy. Caffeine is a stimulant. It blocks adenosine, the brain chemical that builds up during the day and makes you feel tired, so you feel more awake and alert.

You might expect them to cancel out. They don't. Caffeine mostly cancels the *sleepiness*. It doesn't cancel the impairment. Your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is the same whether you drink vodka with soda or vodka with Red Bull. Caffeine doesn't help your liver clear alcohol any faster, so it does nothing to sober you up.

That mismatch is where the problems start:

1. **You lose your natural brake.** For most people, getting tired is the signal that the night is ending. Take that away and it's easy to keep drinking past the point you normally would.
2. **You misjudge how impaired you are.** Feeling alert makes people think they're fine to drive, swim, climb, or get into an argument when they're not.
3. **Your heart gets pushed from both sides.** Both caffeine and alcohol can raise heart rate and, in some people, trigger irregular rhythms. Large energy drinks stack a lot of caffeine on top.
4. **Your sleep gets wrecked.** Alcohol already fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Caffeine delays sleep at the start. You get the worst of both.

## The "Wide-Awake Drunk" Effect: What the Research Shows

The idea that caffeine masks drunkenness isn't just a theory. It has been tested in lab studies for close to two decades.

**Caffeine changes how drunk you feel, not how drunk you are.** In a well-known 2006 study published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, researchers in Brazil gave volunteers alcohol with and without an energy drink. When the energy drink was added, people reported feeling less of some effects of intoxication, such as headache, weakness, and dry mouth, and felt less impaired in their coordination. But objective tests showed their motor coordination and breath alcohol levels were no better. They felt more sober than they were.

**It can make you want to keep drinking.** Lab work led by Cecile Marczinski and colleagues has found that alcohol mixed with an energy drink increased people's desire to keep drinking compared with alcohol alone. That fits what you'd expect when the "I'm done" signal fades.

**Real-world drinking looks riskier too.** Survey research on college students, including a frequently cited 2008 study by O'Brien and colleagues in *Academic Emergency Medicine*, found that students who mixed alcohol with energy drinks reported more heavy drinking and more alcohol-related harms, such as being injured, riding with a drunk driver, or being taken advantage of sexually, than students who drank alcohol without energy drinks. The CDC also notes that people who mix alcohol with energy drinks are more likely to binge drink than people who don't.

There's an important caveat with the survey studies: people who choose to mix energy drinks into their alcohol may already be heavier or riskier drinkers, so the drink isn't necessarily the whole cause. But the lab studies point the same way, and the mechanism makes sense. When the two kinds of evidence agree, it's worth taking seriously.

### Why "I feel fine" is the dangerous part

The most practical takeaway is simple. **When you've had caffeine with alcohol, how you feel is not a reliable gauge of how impaired you are.** Your inner sense of "I'm OK" has been tampered with. Count drinks instead, and set your limit before you start.

This matters most for driving. Feeling wide awake does not restore your reaction time, your ability to judge distance and speed, or your ability to split attention. If you've been drinking, a coffee or an energy drink does not make you safe to drive. Only time does.

## Does Red Bull Have Alcohol?

No. Regular Red Bull, Monster, Rockstar, Celsius, Bang, Reign, and other mainstream energy drinks are non-alcoholic soft drinks. They don't contain added alcohol and you can buy them at any age where they're sold.

The confusion usually comes from two places:

- **The name of the mixed drink.** A "vodka Red Bull," "Red Bull and vodka," or "Jägerbomb" (a shot of Jägermeister dropped into Red Bull) is so common that some people assume Red Bull itself has alcohol in it. It doesn't. The alcohol comes from the spirit.
- **Pre-mixed caffeinated alcoholic drinks.** In the late 2000s, products such as the original Four Loko combined malt liquor with caffeine and other stimulants in a single can. They were linked to a string of hospitalizations, especially among college students. In 2010 the US Food and Drug Administration sent warning letters to several makers of caffeinated alcoholic beverages, saying the caffeine added to their malt drinks was an unsafe food additive. The companies removed the caffeine. Four Loko is still sold, but today's US version is a flavored malt beverage without added caffeine.

So you won't find a legal pre-mixed alcohol-and-caffeine can on US shelves the way you could in 2010. The combination now happens at the bar or at home, when someone mixes it themselves. That's worth knowing, because it means nothing on the label is going to warn you.

## How Much Caffeine Is in Your Mixer?

Energy drinks vary a lot. A small Red Bull has less caffeine than a large coffee, while some newer "performance" energy drinks pack several cups' worth into one can. These are typical figures from US product labels; brands change formulas, so check the can you're holding.

| Drink | Typical size | Approximate caffeine |
|---|---|---|
| Red Bull | 8.4 oz can | about 80 mg |
| Red Bull | 12 oz can | about 114 mg |
| Monster Energy | 16 oz can | about 160 mg |
| Celsius | 12 oz can | about 200 mg |
| Bang or Reign | 16 oz can | about 300 mg |
| Brewed coffee | 8 oz cup | roughly 80 to 100 mg |
| Cola | 12 oz can | roughly 30 to 40 mg |

For comparison, the FDA says that for most healthy adults, up to about **400 mg of caffeine a day** isn't generally associated with dangerous effects. That's a whole-day total, from every source, for a person who isn't drinking.

Now picture a typical night: a coffee in the afternoon, then three vodka Red Bulls from 12 oz cans. That's roughly 425 mg or more, most of it after dark, on top of alcohol. Switch to a 300 mg energy drink as the mixer and you can pass the daily figure in two drinks. Bars rarely tell you which size or brand they're pouring, so you often don't know how much you've had.

### Jägerbombs and shots are the hardest to track

Bombs and shot-style drinks go down fast, usually in rounds, often before people have eaten. You get a quick hit of alcohol and caffeine together, then another round before the first has fully landed. If you're in a group doing rounds, it's fine to sit some out or swap your energy drink for plain soda or water.

## Energy Drinks, Alcohol, and Your Heart

For most healthy people, one energy drink with one drink won't cause a heart problem. The concern is with larger amounts, with people who are sensitive, and with people who have an underlying heart issue they may not know about.

Here's why the combination deserves respect:

- **Caffeine raises heart rate and blood pressure** for a few hours, especially in people who don't drink it often. Big energy drinks deliver a lot at once.
- **Alcohol can trigger irregular heart rhythms.** Doctors have long described "holiday heart syndrome," where a bout of heavy drinking sets off an irregular rhythm, most often atrial fibrillation, in people with otherwise normal hearts.
- **Energy drinks have their own case reports.** Emergency doctors have reported cases of arrhythmias and other heart events linked to heavy energy-drink use, sometimes alongside alcohol. These are uncommon, but they're well enough documented that cardiologists generally advise people with heart conditions to avoid energy drinks.
- **Dehydration and low electrolytes add to it.** Drinking, dancing in a hot room, sweating, and vomiting can all lower potassium and magnesium, which help keep heart rhythm steady.

A pounding, fast heart after a night of mixed drinks is common and usually settles as the caffeine and alcohol wear off. But a racing heart that feels irregular, comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or fainting, or won't settle with rest is a reason to get checked that night. For more on what's normal and what isn't, see our guide to [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

**People who should skip the combination entirely** include anyone with a known heart rhythm problem, structural heart disease, uncontrolled high blood pressure, a history of fainting, panic or anxiety disorder that caffeine worsens, or who is pregnant. If you take prescription stimulants for ADHD, adding an energy drink stacks stimulant on stimulant; ask your doctor before drinking at all.

## Does Mixing Energy Drinks With Alcohol Make Hangovers Worse?

Probably, though mostly indirectly. There's no good evidence that energy drinks prevent a hangover, and several features of the combination make a rough morning more likely.

**You tend to drink more.** This is the biggest factor. Hangover severity tracks closely with how much you drank, and the wide-awake effect makes it easy to drink more than you meant to.

**Your sleep is worse.** Caffeine has a half-life of roughly five hours in a typical adult, which means about half of it is still in your system five hours later, and it can be longer in some people. A midnight energy drink can still be active at 5 a.m. Alcohol, meanwhile, tends to knock you out early and then wake you up in the second half of the night. Poor sleep is a big driver of how bad the next day feels. If that's your pattern, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's happening.

**Sugar and empty stomachs don't help.** Regular energy drinks carry a lot of sugar. Some people drink them instead of eating dinner, which means alcohol is absorbed faster. There's also some research suggesting that sugar-free mixers can lead to a higher breath alcohol level than sugared ones, because sugar slightly slows how fast alcohol leaves the stomach. The practical point isn't "choose the sugary version." It's "eat a real meal first."

**What about dehydration?** Alcohol is a real diuretic. It suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, which is why you pee so much when drinking. Caffeine's diuretic effect is often exaggerated; in people who consume it regularly, moderate amounts don't dehydrate much. So energy drinks aren't adding much dehydration on their own, but they aren't hydrating you either. Every energy drink is one fewer glass of water.

### Can an energy drink help a hangover the next morning?

A small amount of caffeine the next morning can take the edge off grogginess, and if you drink coffee daily it heads off a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of the hangover. That's about the extent of it. A big energy drink on a hangover morning can make nausea, jitteriness, and a racing heart worse, and the sugar crash later in the day doesn't help. If you want caffeine, a normal cup of coffee or tea with food and water is gentler. Energy drinks don't fix the underlying causes of a hangover, and there is no good evidence that they shorten one.

## Why People Mix Them Anyway (and the Myths Behind It)

It's worth being honest about the appeal. People don't mix energy drinks with alcohol because they want to get hurt. They do it because it seems to solve real problems on a night out:

- **"I want to stay out late without getting tired."** It works, in the sense that you'll feel awake. The catch is that staying out later usually means drinking more, with your judgment still impaired.
- **"It tastes better than straight vodka."** Fair. But plenty of mixers taste fine without 100 to 300 mg of caffeine. Soda water with citrus, ginger ale, tonic, or juice all work.
- **"Caffeine will sober me up."** It won't. Your BAC drops at the rate your liver clears alcohol, roughly one standard drink an hour for many people, and nothing in a can speeds that up.
- **"I'll be fine to drive because I feel alert."** This is the most dangerous myth on the list. Alertness and driving ability are not the same thing.
- **"It's just one Red Bull."** One 8.4 oz Red Bull is about the same as a cup of coffee. The problems usually come from the third or fourth, or from a 300 mg can treated like a soft drink.

## The Same Problem in Other Forms

Energy drinks are the most obvious example, but the same masking effect can happen with other caffeine sources:

- **Espresso martinis and coffee cocktails.** A shot of espresso has roughly 60 to 75 mg of caffeine. One is not a big deal. Several over a night add up.
- **Rum and Coke or whiskey and Coke.** Cola has far less caffeine, so this matters much less, but it isn't zero.
- **Pre-workout powders and caffeine pills.** Some people take these before going out. These can carry as much as or more caffeine than an energy drink and should not be mixed with alcohol.
- **Caffeinated hard seltzers or "energy" cocktails at bars.** Read menus and labels where you can, especially when traveling, because rules on caffeinated alcoholic products differ by country.

The principle is the same everywhere: the more caffeine you add, the more your sense of "how drunk am I" drifts away from reality.

## A Safer Way to Handle a Night Out

If you've read this far, you probably still want to have a good night, and that's reasonable. A few habits keep most of the fun and cut most of the risk.

1. **Pick a non-caffeinated mixer.** Soda water, tonic, ginger beer, or juice. If you really want the flavor, have one energy-drink mixer, early in the night, and switch after that.
2. **Decide your number before you start.** Because caffeine distorts how drunk you feel, set your drink limit in advance and count. Many people find it easier to track with a note on their phone.
3. **Eat a proper meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood and makes the night easier on your stomach.
4. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows you down and offsets some fluid loss.
5. **Cut off caffeine several hours before bed.** Give yourself a fighting chance at sleep.
6. **Plan the ride home before you go out.** Rideshare, a designated driver, or public transit. Never drive after mixing caffeine and alcohol, no matter how alert you feel.
7. **Watch your friends.** Someone who is wide-awake drunk can seem fine until they suddenly aren't. If a friend gets confused, vomits repeatedly, or can't be woken, treat it as an emergency.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the evidence behind these habits in more detail.

## Signs of Trouble: When to Get Help Right Away

Most nights with a couple of mixed drinks end with nothing worse than poor sleep. But two kinds of emergency are more likely when caffeine and alcohol are combined, and both need fast action.

**Possible heart rhythm problem. Call 911 or get to an emergency room if someone has:**

- Chest pain, pressure, or tightness
- A very fast, fluttering, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle after resting
- Fainting, near-fainting, or severe dizziness
- Shortness of breath at rest

**Possible alcohol poisoning. Call 911 if someone has:**

- Confusion or stupor, or can't be woken up
- Vomiting while semi-conscious, or repeated vomiting
- Slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about eight breaths a minute, or long gaps between breaths)
- Seizures
- Pale or bluish, cold, clammy skin
- A very low body temperature

Don't let someone "sleep it off" if they show these signs, and don't try to sober them up with more caffeine or a cold shower. Turn them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and call for help. In the US, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) can also advise you if you're unsure.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

Because this site focuses on dihydromyricetin (DHM), it's fair to address it directly. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's an interesting area, but the evidence is early.

Here's what matters for this topic: **DHM does not counteract caffeine, does not lower your BAC to a safe level, and does not make it safe to drive or to mix energy drinks with alcohol.** There is no good evidence that any supplement protects your heart from the caffeine-plus-alcohol combination.

If you drink occasionally and want to try DHM as part of an overall plan that also includes eating, pacing, water, and sleep, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) as a simple budget pick and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) as a multi-ingredient option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and ask your pharmacist first.

The most effective step for a better morning after an energy-drink night is still the simplest one: leave the energy drink out of the glass.

## The Bottom Line

- Energy drinks don't make you less drunk. They make you feel less drunk, which is why the combination leads people to drink more and take more risks.
- Your BAC, reaction time, and judgment are just as impaired with caffeine as without it. Never drive after mixing them.
- Red Bull and other mainstream energy drinks contain no alcohol. The alcohol comes from the spirit you mix in. Pre-mixed caffeinated alcoholic drinks were pushed off the US market after FDA action in 2010.
- Large energy drinks can carry 200 to 300 mg of caffeine each, so a few mixed drinks can exceed a normal day's caffeine.
- The combination is harder on your heart and your sleep, and there is no good evidence that it prevents a hangover.
- If someone has chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, fainting, confusion, or can't be woken up, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it bad to mix energy drinks with alcohol?**

It's riskier than drinking alcohol alone. The caffeine masks the sleepiness that normally tells you you've had enough, so you feel more sober than you are, which tends to lead to more drinking and riskier choices. It also adds strain on your heart and disrupts sleep. One small energy drink with one drink is unlikely to harm a healthy adult, but the safest choice is a non-caffeinated mixer.

**Does Red Bull have alcohol in it?**

No. Red Bull is a non-alcoholic energy drink. In drinks like a vodka Red Bull or a Jägerbomb, the alcohol comes from the spirit that's mixed in. The same is true for Monster, Rockstar, Celsius, and other mainstream energy drinks.

**What does "wide-awake drunk" mean?**

It's the term researchers use for the state of being intoxicated but feeling alert because of caffeine. Lab studies have found that adding an energy drink to alcohol makes people feel less impaired without improving their actual coordination or lowering their breath alcohol level. The danger is that people trust the alert feeling and drive or keep drinking.

**Does caffeine sober you up?**

No. Caffeine can make you feel more awake, but it doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, so your blood alcohol level stays the same. Only time lowers your BAC, at roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, though this varies. Coffee or an energy drink does not make you safe to drive.

**How many vodka Red Bulls is too many?**

There's no single safe number, but a sensible approach is to keep it to one energy-drink mixer and switch to a non-caffeinated mixer after that. Remember that both the alcohol and the caffeine add up: three 12 oz Red Bulls is around 340 mg of caffeine, and some other energy drinks carry 300 mg in a single can. Set your total drink limit before you start, because the caffeine will make you feel less drunk than you are.

**Can energy drinks and alcohol cause a heart attack?**

In healthy young people, serious heart events from this combination are uncommon. But both caffeine and heavy drinking can trigger irregular heart rhythms, and emergency doctors have reported cases linked to large amounts of energy drinks, sometimes with alcohol. People with heart conditions, high blood pressure, or a history of fainting should avoid the combination. Chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, or fainting after drinking needs emergency care.

**Are energy drinks good for a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that energy drinks cure or shorten a hangover. A modest amount of caffeine the next morning can ease grogginess and prevent a caffeine-withdrawal headache if you drink coffee daily, but a large, sugary energy drink can worsen nausea, jitters, and a racing heart. A normal cup of coffee or tea with food and water is a gentler choice.

**Why was Four Loko banned?**

The original Four Loko combined malt liquor with caffeine and other stimulants and was linked to hospitalizations, especially among college students. In 2010 the FDA warned several makers of caffeinated alcoholic drinks that the added caffeine was an unsafe food additive, and the companies removed it. Four Loko is still sold in the US, but without added caffeine.
